title: How IAS Officer Tukaram Mundhe's 3,000 Food Raids Are Reshaping Mumbai's Restaurant Industry
excerpt: Maharashtra's FDA Commissioner has suspended licences of Domino's, Pizza Hut, and McDonald's outlets, inspected Bombay High Court canteens, and turned food safety into a viral public movement.
body:
• IAS officer Tukaram Mundhe has overseen more than 3,000 food safety raids across Maharashtra since taking charge as FDA Commissioner in May 2026, suspending licences of major chains including Domino's, Pizza Hut, and McDonald's.
  • His team has conducted 1,100+ inspections, cancelled 56 restaurant licences, seized Rs 50 crore worth of unsafe food, sealed 322 establishments, and arrested 457 people.
  • Inspections have extended to Bombay High Court canteens, elite clubs like the Cricket Club of India, quick-commerce warehouses of Blinkit and Zepto, and Bollywood's Film City cafeteria.
  • Street vendors across Mumbai have begun changing practices — swapping artificial dyes for natural chilli, changing frying oil more frequently, and using butter paper instead of newspapers.

Tukaram Mundhe does not behave like a typical Indian bureaucrat. Since taking over as Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration Commissioner in May, the 51-year-old IAS officer has led an unprecedented food safety crackdown across the state — one that has shut iconic Mumbai eateries, suspended multinational fast-food outlets, and turned graphic images of cockroach-infested kitchens into viral public reckoning.

From Domino's to the Bombay High Court

The scale of Mundhe's operation is hard to overstate. In roughly three months, his teams have conducted over 3,000 raids across Maharashtra. Four Domino's outlets and one Pizza Hut location had their food permits suspended. On August 22, a McDonald's outlet was shut after inspectors found "live pest activity (cockroaches)" and "rotting food," according to Reuters. McDonald's India said it has "a zero-tolerance approach" to food safety issues.

When a Mumbai judge accused Mundhe of selectively targeting private establishments and asked whether court canteens had been checked, his teams inspected the Bombay High Court's canteens within hours — finding two kitchens operating without valid licences.

"Those who try to not comply, they will face what is expected from the regulator. You are dealing with the lives of people."

— Tukaram Mundhe, FDA Commissioner, Maharashtra

The crackdown has also reached elite institutions. K Rustom Ice Cream Parlour, a 70-year-old Mumbai landmark, and the Cricket Club of India both had their licences suspended. A 110-year-old Parsi Dairy was inspected. The FDA's Bollywood Café raid at Film City in Goregaon East uncovered severe fly infestation, dirty drains, and food prepared on rusty surfaces.

Quick Commerce Under the Scanner

Mundhe's sweep has not spared the booming quick-commerce sector. FDA teams inspected 86 warehouses and fulfilment centres run by Zepto, Blinkit, and Instamart. The inspections resulted in 14 licence suspensions, 60 improvement notices, and one order to halt operations immediately. Blinkit's Malad West facility was shut after cold storage temperatures were found at 6°C — above safe levels — alongside missing medical fitness records for 40 food handlers.

The Officer Who Gets Transferred Every Year

Mundhe's combative approach is not new. In 21 years with the Indian Administrative Service, he has been transferred 25 times — a record that, as the Hindustan Times noted, has come to define his public identity as much as his work. He has declared in TV interviews that nobody dares bribe him, and that he does not fear administrative action.

"I have never seen anyone like Mundhe. It's giving people hope."

— Ankur Bisen, partner at consumer consulting firm The Knowledge Company

Dubbed "Singham" — after the Ajay Devgn film about an uncompromising police officer — Mundhe has become something of a folk hero. At a New Delhi event on August 22, fans lined up for selfies and handshakes. One told him Prime Minister Modi should give him a national role. "I don't think I'm a celebrity. I'm just a food safety commissioner," Mundhe told Reuters.

Real Change on Mumbai's Streets

Reuters visits to 25 Mumbai street vendors and restaurants found heightened awareness. One vendor swapped artificial red dye for natural chilli in Chinese food offerings. Another started changing frying oil three times daily and required staff to wear gloves and head caps. Mundhe's June ban on newspapers as food packaging — widely used for vada pav — pushed vendors to switch to butter paper. Fourteen-year-old customer Supriya Wagle said the cleaner packaging is "surely a relief."

Government data tells the broader story: each year since 2020, Indian food inspectors have checked more than 100,000 food samples and found roughly 20% to be unsafe, substandard, or lacking proper labels. Nearly 8,000 food business licences have been cancelled in the last three years.

Pushback and What Comes Next

Not everyone is cheering. Some businesses have accused the FDA of high-handedness and approached the Bombay High Court. In one case, judges fined Mundhe's department Rs 5 lakh for continuing to suspend an eatery that had improved its compliance. "If there are observations by the court, we take it seriously," Mundhe said.

Whether Mundhe's crackdown produces lasting systemic change or fades with his next transfer remains an open question. But for now, Mumbai's kitchens are cleaner than they have been in years — and the public is watching.
image_caption: IAS officer Tukaram Mundhe, who has led over 3,000 food safety raids across Mumbai, reshaping the city's restaurant industry with strict enforcement of hygiene standards.
nri_angle: The crackdown resonates with NRIs who frequently raise concerns about food hygiene standards in India, particularly at restaurants and street food stalls they visit during trips home.
